q.s: A 42-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis has had progressive exertional dyspnea for a year. Blood pressure is 168/48 mm Hg. His head bobs slightly with each heartbeat, and the radial pulse rises and collapses abruptly. A high-pitched blowing early diastolic decrescendo murmur is heard along the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward. The pressure-volume loop from catheterization (dashed) is shown with a normal loop.
o: Reduced contractility shifts the end-systolic point rightward with a small stroke volume
Loss of isovolumetric contraction because blood leaks backward into the left atrium
Ventricular filling begins during relaxation because blood flows back from the aorta, enlarging end-diastolic volume
Impaired filling from a stiff ventricle raises end-diastolic pressure at a normal volume
Restricted filling across a narrowed mitral valve reduces EDV
A high afterload raises the systolic pressure needed to open the aortic valve
e: Correct. In aortic regurgitation there is no true isovolumetric relaxation; regurgitant flow fills the ventricle from the aorta, producing a large EDV and stroke volume (eccentric hypertrophy).
cl: Aortitis and aortic root dilation cause aortic regurgitation.
Wide pulse pressure from large stroke volume and diastolic runoff.
His head bobs slightly with each heartbeat
q.ch: Spondyloarthropathy → aortic root dilation → AR → diastolic backflow fills LV (no isovolumetric relaxation) → large EDV and SV → wide pulse pressure with bounding pulses.
q.tr: AR = "Always Rushing back": big volume in, big volume out, big pulse pressure.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the shape of this patient's loop?

q.s: A 19-year-old college student has had episodes of rapid palpitations since childhood. He is asymptomatic now. His resting ECG is shown. He asks what medication he should avoid if he ever develops atrial fibrillation.
o: Amiodarone given for stable ventricular tachycardia
e: Wrong. Not the classic danger in pre-excited AF.
Wrong. Can be used to convert AF in WPW.
Wrong. Procainamide slows accessory pathway conduction and is preferred.
Wrong. The treatment of unstable pre-excited AF.
Wrong. Curative treatment of the pathway.

Correct. This is Wolff-Parkinson-White (short PR, delta wave). AV nodal blockers such as verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin and adenosine can push atrial fibrillation down the accessory pathway, causing very fast ventricular rates or ventricular fibrillation.
cl: Recurrent re-entrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway.
if he ever develops atrial fibrillation
Pre-excited AF is the dangerous situation in WPW.
Pre-excitation is seen on the resting ECG between episodes.
q.ch: Short PR + delta wave → accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) → in AF, blocking the AV node sends impulses down the pathway → very rapid rates → avoid AV nodal blockers; use procainamide or cardioversion.
q.tr: In WPW with AF, "ABCD — Avoid": Adenosine, β-blockers, Calcium channel blockers, Digoxin.
q.q2: Which drug is most dangerous if he develops atrial fibrillation?

q.s: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes reports intermittent palpitations for a week. She has no history of stroke or bleeding. Pulse is 104/min and irregularly irregular. Creatinine is normal. Her rhythm strip is shown. Rate control is started.
e: Wrong. Aspirin is inadequate for stroke prevention in AF.
Correct. A direct factor Xa inhibitor is preferred for stroke prevention in nonvalvular AF with a high CHA2DS2-VASc score.
Wrong. Thrombolysis treats acute stroke or MI.
Wrong. Her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5 (age ≥75 = 2, female = 1, hypertension = 1, diabetes = 1); anticoagulation is indicated.
Wrong. Not appropriate for long-term outpatient prevention.
cl: 76-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes
no history of stroke or bleeding
q.ch: Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves → AF → stasis in the left atrial appendage → thromboembolic stroke risk (high CHA2DS2-VASc) → anticoagulate with a DOAC (factor Xa inhibitor).
q.tr: CHA2DS2-VASc: CHF, HTN, Age ≥75 (2), Diabetes, Stroke (2), Vascular disease, Age 65–74, Sex category (female).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to prevent stroke in this patient?

q.s: A 34-year-old woman has had progressive exertional dyspnea and fatigue for 2 years. She fainted once while climbing stairs. There is a loud P2, a right ventricular heave and a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. The liver is pulsatile. Echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 75 mm Hg; left heart function is normal. Her jugular venous tracing is shown. Her mother died of a similar illness.
e: Correct. Heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension is most often due to inactivating BMPR2 mutations, causing smooth muscle proliferation in pulmonary arterioles; RV pressure overload leads to tricuspid regurgitation (giant c-v waves).
cl: Systolic backflow into the hepatic veins.
Pre-capillary (pulmonary arterial) hypertension, not left heart disease.
Her mother died of a similar illness
q.ch: Young woman + exertional syncope + loud P2 + RV heave + TR (giant cv waves, pulsatile liver) + normal left heart + family history → heritable PAH → BMPR2 mutation.
q.tr: "BMPR2 = Blood vessels in the lungs Multiply and Proliferate."
q.q2: A mutation in which gene most likely underlies her condition?

q.s: A 45-year-old woman with paroxysmal hypertension, headaches and palpitations has a 4-cm adrenal mass and markedly elevated plasma metanephrines. In a preclinical study, the effect of two drugs (X and Y) on norepinephrine-induced vascular smooth muscle contraction is tested; the dose-response curves are shown. Before surgery, she is given drug Y.
e: Wrong. A reversible competitive α-antagonist shifts the curve right without lowering the maximum (drug X).
Wrong. A β-blocker does not block α1-mediated vasoconstriction and should not be given first.
Wrong. A reversible competitive α1-antagonist (parallel right shift).
Correct. An irreversible α-antagonist lowers the maximal response (noncompetitive pattern); it is used before resecting a pheochromocytoma.
cl: Before surgery, she is given drug Y
α-blockade must be complete before resection.
q.ch: Pheochromocytoma → preoperative irreversible α-blockade → phenoxybenzamine → noncompetitive pattern (↓ maximal response) vs a competitive antagonist (↑ EC50, same maximum).
q.tr: "Competitive shifts right; Irreversible pushes down."
q.q2: Drug Y is most likely which of the following?
q.fc: Dose-response curves for norepinephrine on vascular smooth muscle

q.s: A 6-year-old boy who has been profoundly deaf since birth collapses after being startled by a loud alarm at school. He regains consciousness after 30 seconds. His parents are first cousins and have normal hearing. His resting ECG is shown.
o: Phase 4, by increasing the funny current
Phase 0, by increasing Ca2+ influx in the AV node
Phase 1, by increasing transient outward Cl− current
Phase 3, by reducing delayed rectifier K+ efflux
Phase 0, by reducing fast Na+ influx
e: Correct. Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (autosomal recessive, with sensorineural deafness) results from loss of K+ channel function (eg, KCNQ1), delaying repolarization and prolonging QT, predisposing to torsades.
Wrong. Loss of Na+ current is seen in Brugada syndrome.
cl: Congenital sensorineural deafness: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome.
Adrenergic triggers provoke arrhythmia in long QT.
Consanguinity points to autosomal recessive inheritance.
q.ch: Deaf child + syncope with startle + consanguinity + long QT → Jervell and Lange-Nielsen → loss of K+ channel function → slow phase 3 repolarization → torsades.
q.tr: "Jervell: Just very long QT, plus deaf"; Romano-Ward is the "Regular" (dominant, hearing normal) form.
q.q2: The underlying defect most directly affects which phase of the ventricular action potential?

q.s: A 28-year-old woman has sudden palpitations and light-headedness while drinking coffee at work. Pulse is 186/min and regular. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Carotid sinus massage is unsuccessful. Her rhythm strip is shown. A rapid intravenous bolus of a drug terminates the rhythm after a few seconds of asystole.
o: Blocking voltage-gated Na+ channels in the His-Purkinje system
Blocking L-type Ca2+ channels for several hours
Activating A1 receptors that increase K+ efflux and hyperpolarize AV nodal cells
Blocking β1 receptors in the SA node
Increasing vagal tone through central muscarinic stimulation
e: Wrong. That is a class I drug action.
Wrong. Verapamil works this way but is not ultrashort.
Correct. Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node, interrupting AV nodal re-entry; its effect is blunted by caffeine and theophylline (adenosine receptor antagonists).
cl: Caffeine antagonizes adenosine receptors; higher doses may be needed.
Ultrashort AV block typical of adenosine.
q.ch: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia + failed vagal maneuver → adenosine → A1 receptors → ↑ K+ efflux, ↓ Ca2+ current → transient AV block → re-entry stops.
q.tr: "Adenosine: A-stop for 6 seconds"; caffeine and theophylline "Cancel" it.
q.q2: The drug given acts mainly through which mechanism?

q.s: A 33-year-old woman has occasional palpitations and atypical chest pain. She is thin with a high-arched palate. A midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is heard at the apex. Over 10 years, the regurgitation becomes severe. Simultaneous left heart pressure tracings at that time are shown.
e: Wrong. Increases preload, so the click moves later.
Correct. Reduced preload makes the LV smaller, so the redundant mitral leaflets prolapse earlier, moving the click toward S1.
Wrong. Increases afterload and LV size, delaying the click.
q.k: Mitral valve prolapse and mitral regurgitation
cl: Connective tissue features associated with myxomatous valve disease.
midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur
Chronic MR raises left atrial v waves (tracing).
q.ch: Thin woman + click and late systolic murmur → mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration) → less LV volume = earlier prolapse; severe MR shows a large LA v wave.
q.tr: MVP and HOCM both "hate a small heart": less preload makes the click earlier and the HOCM murmur louder.
q.q2: Which maneuver would make the click occur earlier in systole?
q.fc: Simultaneous LV, aortic and left atrial pressures

q.s: A cardiac physiologist measures a resting adult's values during catheterization, shown in the table. Whole-body oxygen consumption is measured by spirometry, arterial oxygen content from a radial artery sample, and mixed venous oxygen content from a pulmonary artery sample.
e: Wrong. This divides the arterial-venous difference by O2 consumption.
Wrong. Not consistent with the Fick calculation.
Correct. Fick principle: CO = O2 consumption / (arterial − venous O2 content) = 250 / (200 − 150) = 5 L/min.
Wrong. Not consistent with the values.
Wrong. This divides by venous content minus a tenth.
cl: Arterial minus venous content gives O2 extracted per liter.
mixed venous oxygen content from a pulmonary artery sample
Mixed venous blood must come from the pulmonary artery, where all venous blood has mixed.
q.ch: Fick: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 − CvO2) = 250 mL/min ÷ 50 mL/L = 5 L/min; heart rate and hemoglobin are distractors.
q.tr: "Fick = what the body Takes ÷ what each liter Gives."
q.q2: What is this person's cardiac output?

q.s: A 70-year-old man with recurrent atrial fibrillation is started on a drug that prolongs the action potential mainly by blocking K+ channels without affecting the upstroke. The labeled ventricular action potential is shown. The drug requires in-hospital initiation with QT monitoring and dose adjustment for creatinine clearance.
e: Wrong. β-blockers decrease phase 4 slope in nodal cells.
Wrong. Class IB shortens phase 3 and acts on Na+ channels.
Correct. A class III K+ channel blocker prolongs repolarization (phase 3) and the QT interval; it is started in hospital with QT and renal monitoring.
Wrong. Class IC slows phase 0 markedly.
Wrong. Class IV drugs act mainly on nodal tissue.
cl: blocking K+ channels without affecting the upstroke
q.ch: K+ channel blockade → slower phase 3 repolarization → longer action potential and QT → class III (dofetilide) → torsades risk, needs monitored initiation.
q.tr: Class III = "AIDS": Amiodarone, Ibutilide, Dofetilide, Sotalol — they all prolong phase 3.
q.q2: Which drug was most likely started, and which phase does it prolong?
q.fc: Ventricular action potential with phases labeled

q.s: A 41-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the right arm and face. She had a long flight 2 days ago and has a swollen, tender left calf. A soft systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border, and S2 is widely split and does not vary with respiration. MRI confirms an acute stroke.
o: Paradoxical embolism of a venous thrombus through an atrial septal defect
Embolism of a left atrial thrombus from atrial fibrillation
Atherosclerotic plaque rupture in the carotid artery
e: Correct. Fixed wide splitting of S2 suggests an atrial septal defect; a DVT can cross the interatrial communication into the systemic circulation.
Wrong. No positional symptoms or mass described.
Wrong. No irregular rhythm is described.
Wrong. Unlikely at her age without risk factors, and does not explain the DVT link.
q.k: Atrial septal defect with paradoxical embolism
cl: Venous stasis and deep vein thrombosis.
widely split and does not vary with respiration
Fixed splitting of S2: atrial septal defect.
soft systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border
Increased flow across the pulmonic valve.
q.ch: DVT + fixed split S2 + pulmonic flow murmur → ASD → venous clot crosses the atrial septum → arterial (cerebral) embolism.
q.tr: "Fixed split = Fixed hole in the atrial wall."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains how she developed a stroke?

q.s: A 32-year-old man who emigrated as an adult has never had medical care. He reports fatigue and dyspnea. His fingers are normal, but his toes are cyanotic and clubbed. Oxygen saturation is 98% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot. A loud P2 is heard; no continuous murmur is present.
o: Reversal of flow across a patent ductus arteriosus from pulmonary hypertension
Peripheral arterial disease of the legs
A large ventricular septal defect with right-to-left shunt
Coarctation of the aorta proximal to the left subclavian artery
e: Correct. Eisenmenger physiology in an uncorrected PDA sends deoxygenated pulmonary artery blood into the aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, causing cyanosis and clubbing of the lower extremities only.
Wrong. Would not lower arterial oxygen saturation.
Wrong. Would cause cyanosis of both upper and lower extremities.
cl: his toes are cyanotic and clubbed
98% in the right hand and 84% in the left foot
Desaturated blood enters below the left subclavian artery.
The PDA murmur disappears when pulmonary and aortic pressures equalize.
q.ch: Untreated PDA → years of L→R flow → pulmonary vascular remodeling → pulmonary hypertension → shunt reverses (Eisenmenger) → deoxygenated blood to lower body → cyanotic, clubbed toes with normal fingers.
q.tr: PDA Eisenmenger = "blue toes, pink fingers."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains the differential cyanosis?

q.s: A newborn is cyanotic shortly after birth. His mother took a medication for bipolar disorder throughout pregnancy. Echocardiography shows apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets with atrialization of the right ventricle and severe tricuspid regurgitation.
e: Wrong. Associated with neural tube defects and craniofacial anomalies.
Wrong. Associated with neural tube defects.
Correct. First-trimester lithium exposure is associated with Ebstein anomaly.
cl: Lithium is a classic mood stabilizer.
apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets
Part of the RV functions as atrium.
q.ch: Maternal mood stabilizer + newborn with downward-displaced tricuspid valve and severe TR → Ebstein anomaly → lithium.
q.tr: "Lithium makes the tricuspid Lie low" (Ebstein).
q.q2: Which medication did the mother most likely take?

q.s: A 2-day-old boy has cyanosis, a holosystolic murmur and a seizure. Serum calcium is 6.4 mg/dL. Chest radiography shows absence of the thymic shadow. Echocardiography shows a single large vessel arising from both ventricles above a ventricular septal defect.
o: Cardiac jelly of the septum primum
e: Correct. 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge syndrome) impairs neural crest migration into the truncus and conotruncal ridges, causing persistent truncus arteriosus and other outflow defects, plus 3rd/4th pouch defects (thymic and parathyroid aplasia).
cl: a single large vessel arising from both ventricles
q.ch: Neonatal hypocalcemia + absent thymus + conotruncal defect → 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) → failed neural crest migration → truncus arteriosus failed to divide.
q.tr: CATCH-22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, 22q11.
q.q2: Abnormal development of which cell population best explains this infant's cardiac defect?

q.s: A newborn girl has upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, a single palmar crease and hypotonia. A murmur is heard, and echocardiography shows a defect involving both the lower atrial septum and the upper ventricular septum with a common atrioventricular valve.
e: Wrong. Ostium secundum ASD or PFO.
Correct. Atrioventricular septal defects result from failed fusion of the endocardial cushions and are strongly associated with Down syndrome.
q.k: AV septal defect in Down syndrome
cl: upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, a single palmar crease and hypotonia
both the lower atrial septum and the upper ventricular septum
The crux of the heart formed by the endocardial cushions.
q.ch: Down syndrome phenotype + defect at the heart's crux with common AV valve → AV septal (endocardial cushion) defect.
q.tr: Down syndrome "Cushions" the heart badly: endocardial cushion defects.
q.q2: Failure of which embryologic structure most likely caused this cardiac defect?

q.s: A 72-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history and hypertension has a pulsatile, nontender epigastric mass. Ultrasonography shows a 5.8-cm infrarenal aortic dilation. He has no symptoms.
o: Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch
Transmural inflammation with matrix metalloproteinase degradation of elastin and collagen
Intimal tear with blood dissecting the media
Endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum
Cystic medial degeneration from fibrillin defects
e: Correct. Abdominal aortic aneurysms are associated with atherosclerosis and smoking; inflammation and MMPs weaken the media.
Wrong. Typical of thoracic aortic disease in Marfan syndrome.
cl: Smoking is the strongest risk factor for AAA.
q.ch: Elderly male smoker + pulsatile epigastric mass + infrarenal dilation → AAA → atherosclerosis-related inflammation, MMP activity → weakened media.
q.tr: AAA = "Aging Arteries from Ash" (smoking); screen men 65–75 who ever smoked.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this lesion?

q.s: A pathologist examines the aorta of a 19-year-old man who died in a motor vehicle collision. He had no known medical problems. There are flat yellow streaks on the intimal surface that do not protrude into the lumen.
o: Smooth muscle cells forming a fibrous cap
Macrophages filled with oxidized LDL (foam cells)
e: Wrong. Not the characteristic early event.
Correct. Fatty streaks, the earliest visible lesions of atherosclerosis, consist of lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) after endothelial dysfunction and LDL oxidation.
cl: Fatty streaks begin in childhood and adolescence.
flat yellow streaks on the intimal surface
do not protrude into the lumen
q.ch: Endothelial injury → LDL enters and is oxidized → monocytes enter and become foam cells → fatty streak → later smooth muscle migration and fibrous cap.
q.tr: Atherosclerosis order: "Endothelium hurt → Foam → Fibrous cap → Fracture (rupture)."
q.q2: The earliest cellular event in the formation of these lesions is accumulation of which of the following in the intima?

q.s: A 36-year-old woman who smokes has had episodes of chest pain at 4 AM that wake her from sleep and last 10 minutes. During one episode, an ECG shows ST elevation in the inferior leads that resolves completely within minutes. Coronary angiography shows normal coronary arteries. She also has migraines.
e: Correct. Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina is treated with calcium channel blockers (and nitrates); smoking cessation helps.
Wrong. Triptans cause coronary vasospasm and should be avoided.
Wrong. Nonselective β-blockade leaves α-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can worsen vasospasm.
cl: chest pain at 4 AM that wake her from sleep
Resting, early-morning episodes typical of vasospasm.
ST elevation in the inferior leads that resolves completely within minutes
q.ch: Young smoker + nocturnal rest angina + transient ST elevation + normal coronaries → coronary vasospasm → CCBs and nitrates; avoid nonselective β-blockers and triptans.
q.tr: Prinzmetal "Prefers Ca channel blockers"; triggers: smoking, cocaine, triptans.
q.q2: Which drug is most appropriate to prevent these episodes?

q.s: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with chest pain 1 hour after snorting cocaine. He is agitated and diaphoretic. Temperature is 38.2°C, pulse 128/min and blood pressure 176/108 mm Hg. Pupils are dilated. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST elevation. Aspirin is given.
e: Wrong. Lowers seizure threshold and impairs heat dissipation.
Wrong. β-blockers are avoided in acute cocaine toxicity because unopposed α-stimulation can worsen hypertension and vasospasm.
Correct. Benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic outflow, lowering heart rate, blood pressure and agitation; nitrates and calcium channel blockers can be added.
q.ch: Cocaine → blocks catecholamine reuptake → tachycardia, hypertension, coronary vasospasm → benzodiazepines first, avoid β-blockers.
q.tr: Cocaine chest pain: "Benzos Before Blockers (never β first)."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next pharmacotherapy?

q.s: A 66-year-old man is treated with a stent for an acute anterior myocardial infarction. Four days later he develops recurrent chest pain with new ST elevation. Cardiac troponin I remains elevated from the initial event.
e: Correct. CK-MB rises within hours and returns to normal in 48–72 hours, so a new rise after day 3 indicates reinfarction.
Wrong. Reflects ventricular stretch, not infarction.
Wrong. Stays elevated for 7–10 days, so it cannot easily distinguish a new event at day 4.
cl: Reinfarction window after initial markers peak.
troponin I remains elevated from the initial event
q.ch: Recurrent pain day 4 + troponin already high → need a marker that normalizes quickly → CK-MB re-rise means reinfarction.
q.tr: "Troponin Tarries (7–10 days); CK-MB Comes and goes (2–3 days)."
q.q2: Which serum marker is most useful to confirm a new (re-)infarction?

q.s: A 61-year-old man had a myocardial infarction 4 weeks ago. He now has fever, pleuritic chest pain that improves when he leans forward, and a three-component friction rub. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. ESR is elevated.
o: Autoimmune reaction to myocardial antigens released by necrosis
e: Wrong. Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression indicates pericarditis.
Wrong. Occurs 3–14 days after MI with tamponade.
Wrong. Would be more acute with purulence.
Correct. Dressler syndrome (postcardiac injury syndrome) is an autoimmune fibrinous pericarditis weeks after MI.
Wrong. Causes persistent ST elevation, heart failure and thrombi, not fever with a rub.
cl: Dressler syndrome occurs weeks to months after MI.
diffuse ST elevation with PR depression
q.ch: MI weeks ago → myocardial antigens exposed → autoimmune pericarditis (Dressler) → fever, positional pleuritic pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation → NSAIDs/colchicine.
q.tr: Post-MI pericarditis: "early (days) = fibrinous over the infarct; late (weeks) = Dressler, the Delayed autoimmune one."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his current condition?

q.s: A 58-year-old man undergoes successful primary angioplasty 5 hours after the onset of an anterior myocardial infarction. He dies of a ventricular arrhythmia 12 hours later. Microscopic examination of the reperfused myocardium shows hypereosinophilic transverse bands across myocytes and areas of hemorrhage.
o: Calcium influx after restoration of blood flow causing hypercontraction
e: Wrong. Not the explanation for bands.
Correct. Reperfusion injury: Ca2+ influx and free radicals cause contraction band necrosis and hemorrhage.
q.ch: Reperfusion of injured myocardium → Ca2+ influx and oxygen free radicals → hypercontraction → contraction band necrosis and hemorrhage.
q.tr: "Reperfusion Restores blood, but brings Calcium and Radicals."
q.q2: These findings are most directly caused by which of the following?

q.s: A 45-year-old man who grew up in a rural adobe house in Bolivia has palpitations, dyspnea and severe constipation. Examination shows an enlarged heart with an S3. Barium enema shows a markedly dilated colon, and barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus. ECG shows right bundle branch block.
e: Correct. Chagas disease, transmitted by the reduviid (kissing) bug, causes dilated cardiomyopathy and destruction of enteric neurons (megacolon, megaesophagus).
Wrong. Myocarditis without megacolon or megaesophagus.
cl: Exposure to reduviid bugs living in cracks of mud walls.
q.ch: Latin American rural exposure + dilated cardiomyopathy + megacolon + megaesophagus → Chagas disease → Trypanosoma cruzi (treat with benznidazole or nifurtimox).
q.tr: "Chagas: Cardiomegaly + Colon + Esophagus — the Kissing bug's 3 big organs."
q.q2: Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

q.s: A 52-year-old woman with breast cancer completed chemotherapy 1 year ago. She now has progressive dyspnea, orthopnea and leg edema. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30%. She received a cumulative high dose of one agent.
e: Correct. Anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiotoxicity is dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy from free radicals; dexrazoxane, an iron chelator, reduces it.
Wrong. Rescues normal cells from methotrexate.
cl: Anthracyclines are part of many breast cancer regimens.
cumulative high dose of one agent
q.ch: Breast cancer chemotherapy → high cumulative doxorubicin → free radical myocyte injury → irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy → prevent with dexrazoxane.
q.tr: "DOXorubicin breaks the heart; DEXrazoxane DEfends it."
q.q2: Which drug could have been given with the chemotherapy to reduce this complication?

q.s: A 48-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use disorder has dyspnea, leg edema and warm extremities. Pulse is 112/min and blood pressure 128/52 mm Hg. He has bounding pulses, an S3 and bilateral crackles. He also has numbness of the feet. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with a high cardiac output.
e: Wrong. Causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy but not high-output heart failure.
Correct. Wet beriberi causes high-output heart failure from peripheral vasodilation, plus peripheral neuropathy (dry beriberi).
cl: Main risk factor for thiamine deficiency in high-income settings.
Wide pulse pressure from low SVR.
q.ch: Alcohol → thiamine deficiency → impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-KG dehydrogenase → vasodilation and high-output failure (wet) + neuropathy (dry) → give thiamine.
q.tr: Beriberi = "Ber1 Ber1": vitamin B1; wet = "Wet heart."
q.q2: Deficiency of which vitamin best explains his heart failure?

q.s: A 62-year-old man has dyspnea and a decrescendo diastolic murmur. Chest radiography shows a calcified, dilated ascending aorta. He had a painless genital ulcer decades ago that was never treated. He also has a positive Romberg sign and pupils that accommodate but do not react to light.
o: The elastic lamellae from fibrillin defects
The aortic intima with plaque formation
The aortic valve leaflets from vegetations
The vasa vasorum of the aorta
The adventitia from granulomas in the aortic arch branches
e: Wrong. Atherosclerosis affects mostly the abdominal aorta.
Correct. Tertiary syphilis causes endarteritis obliterans of the vasa vasorum, leading to medial ischemia, "tree bark" aortic wall, ascending aortic aneurysm and aortic regurgitation.
Wrong. Can be involved but are not the primary lesion.
cl: Syphilitic aortitis affects the ascending aorta and arch.
painless genital ulcer decades ago that was never treated
accommodate but do not react to light
q.ch: Untreated syphilis → tertiary stage → endarteritis of vasa vasorum → aortic media ischemia → ascending aortic aneurysm with tree-bark wall → aortic regurgitation; plus tabes and Argyll Robertson pupils.
q.tr: Tertiary syphilis "hits the Big Vessels via the small vessels (vasa vasorum)."
q.q2: The aortic disease is primarily caused by inflammation of which structure?

q.s: A 25-year-old woman has had fatigue, low-grade fever, night sweats and pain in her left arm when combing her hair for 3 months. The left radial pulse is barely palpable, and blood pressure is 88/60 mm Hg in the left arm and 130/80 mm Hg in the right arm. A bruit is heard over the left subclavian artery. ESR is 70 mm/h.
o: Granulomatous inflammation of temporal artery branches in the elderly
Necrotizing vasculitis of medium arteries associated with hepatitis B
Segmental thrombosing vasculitis of small and medium arteries in a smoker
Granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch and its major branches in a young woman
e: Wrong. Unlikely at 25 with constitutional symptoms.
Wrong. Giant cell arteritis affects people over 50.
Correct. Takayasu arteritis ("pulseless disease") is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis, typically in women under 40.
cl: pain in her left arm when combing her hair
88/60 mm Hg in the left arm and 130/80 mm Hg in the right arm
Asymmetric arm pressures from subclavian stenosis.
q.ch: Young woman + constitutional symptoms + arm claudication + weak pulse + BP difference + bruit → Takayasu arteritis (granulomatous aortic arch vasculitis) → glucocorticoids.
q.tr: Takayasu = "Takes away pulses" in young women; giant cell arteritis in the elderly.
q.q2: Which of the following best describes this condition?

q.s: A 34-year-old man who smokes two packs of cigarettes daily has painful ulcers on the tips of several fingers and toes and pain in his calves when walking. He has had recurrent tender cordlike nodules along superficial veins of his legs. Angiography shows segmental occlusions of small and medium arteries with corkscrew collaterals.
e: Correct. Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is strongly linked to tobacco; stopping smoking is the only proven way to halt progression and avoid amputation.
cl: smokes two packs of cigarettes daily
painful ulcers on the tips of several fingers and toes
tender cordlike nodules along superficial veins
q.ch: Young heavy smoker + digital ischemia + claudication + superficial thrombophlebitis + segmental occlusions → Buerger disease → smoking cessation.
q.tr: Buerger = "Burning tobacco"; quit or lose digits.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most important treatment?

q.s: A 46-year-old man has chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge, hemoptysis and cola-colored urine. Chest CT shows multiple cavitating nodules. Urinalysis shows red cell casts. A nasal biopsy shows necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis.
o: Glomerular basement membrane type IV collagen
e: Correct. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) is associated with c-ANCA (anti-PR3).
Wrong. Goodpasture syndrome (no granulomas, no sinus disease).
Wrong. MPO-ANCA is associated with microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
cl: chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge
q.ch: Upper airway + lung + kidney involvement with necrotizing granulomas → granulomatosis with polyangiitis → c-ANCA (PR3).
q.tr: GPA hits "ELK": Ears/nose/throat, Lungs, Kidneys; "c-ANCA = Cytoplasmic = PR3."
q.q2: The autoantibody most specific for this disease targets which antigen?

q.s: A 54-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B has fever, weight loss, abdominal pain after meals, new hypertension and painful foot drop. Labs show elevated creatinine; urinalysis has no red cell casts. Chest radiography is normal. Mesenteric angiography shows multiple microaneurysms.
o: Granulomas with giant cells in the aortic arch
Transmural fibrinoid necrosis of medium arteries with lesions of different ages
e: Correct. Polyarteritis nodosa, associated with hepatitis B, causes segmental transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium arteries (sparing the lungs), with microaneurysms.
q.ch: HBV + constitutional symptoms + renal, GI and nerve ischemia + spared lungs + microaneurysms → polyarteritis nodosa → transmural fibrinoid necrosis of medium arteries.
q.tr: PAN: "Pearls (aneurysms), No lungs, Hep B."
q.q2: Biopsy of an affected artery would most likely show which of the following?

q.s: A 6-year-old boy has a raised, nonblanching rash on his buttocks and legs, colicky abdominal pain and painful knees. Two weeks ago he had an upper respiratory infection. Platelet count is normal. Urinalysis shows hematuria.
o: Deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in small vessels
e: Wrong. Immune thrombocytopenia (platelets would be low).
Correct. IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) causes palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain and IgA nephropathy-like glomerulonephritis, often after a URI.
cl: raised, nonblanching rash on his buttocks and legs
Purpura is from vasculitis, not thrombocytopenia.
q.ch: Child + recent URI + palpable purpura with normal platelets + arthralgia + abdominal pain + hematuria → IgA vasculitis (IgA immune complexes).
q.tr: HSP's tetrad: "Purpura, Pain in belly, Polyarthralgia, Pee with blood."
q.q2: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis?

q.s: A 38-year-old woman has episodes in which her fingers turn white, then blue, then red when exposed to cold. She also has tightening skin on her fingers, heartburn and small dilated vessels on her face. Anti-centromere antibodies are positive.
e: Correct. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are first-line for Raynaud phenomenon, here secondary to limited scleroderma (CREST).
cl: Triphasic color change of Raynaud phenomenon.
small dilated vessels on her face
q.ch: Cold-induced triphasic color change + sclerodactyly + esophageal dysmotility + telangiectasia + anti-centromere → CREST with secondary Raynaud → dihydropyridine CCB.
q.tr: CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia.
q.q2: Which drug is the first-line treatment for her color changes?

q.s: A 64-year-old man with hypertension started a new antihypertensive drug 2 months ago. He now has an acutely painful, red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Serum calcium is 10.7 mg/dL and serum glucose is mildly elevated compared with prior values.
e: Wrong. ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalemia and cough, not gout.
Wrong. Losartan modestly lowers uric acid.
Correct. Thiazides cause hyperuricemia (gout), hypercalcemia and hyperglycemia, along with hypokalemia and hyponatremia ("hyperGLUC").
cl: acutely painful, red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint
q.ch: New antihypertensive + gout + hypercalcemia + hyperglycemia → thiazide → "hyperGLUC" (Glycemia, Lipidemia, Uricemia, Calcemia).
q.tr: Thiazides make you "hyperGLUC."
q.q2: Which drug was most likely started?

q.s: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension started a new medication 6 weeks ago. Her blood pressure is now controlled, but she has bilateral ankle swelling that does not improve with furosemide. Serum albumin, liver tests and echocardiography are normal.
o: Amlodipine; preferential arteriolar dilation raising capillary hydrostatic pressure
e: Wrong. Not the mechanism with normal echo.
Correct. Dihydropyridine CCBs dilate precapillary arterioles more than venules, raising capillary pressure; diuretics do not help, but adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB can.
Wrong. Not an antihypertensive here and echo is normal.
Wrong. ACE inhibitors cause angioedema, not dependent edema.
cl: started a new medication 6 weeks ago
q.ch: Antihypertensive + ankle edema resistant to diuretics + normal heart, liver, albumin → dihydropyridine CCB → arteriolar dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure.
q.tr: "Amlodipine: Ankles get big."
q.q2: Which drug most likely caused her edema, and by what mechanism?

q.s: A 58-year-old man with resistant hypertension takes several medications, including one that stimulates central α2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow. He runs out of his pills while traveling. Two days later he has headache, tremor, sweating, anxiety and a blood pressure of 210/120 mm Hg.
e: Correct. Sudden discontinuation causes rebound hypertension and sympathetic overactivity.
Wrong. Causes hypertrichosis and reflex tachycardia, not rebound.
cl: stimulates central α2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow
He runs out of his pills
q.ch: Central α2-agonist stopped abruptly → loss of inhibition → catecholamine surge → rebound hypertensive crisis.
q.tr: "Clonidine: Can't stop suddenly."
q.q2: Abrupt withdrawal of which drug best explains this?

q.s: A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is switched from an ACE inhibitor to a combination tablet containing an angiotensin receptor blocker and a second drug. His physician tells him to wait 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose before starting it.
o: Increases natriuretic peptides by inhibiting neprilysin; washout prevents angioedema from combined bradykinin buildup
Increases potassium excretion; washout prevents hypokalemia
Increases bradykinin by blocking ACE; washout prevents hypotension
Increases cGMP by inhibiting PDE5; washout prevents priapism
Increases aldosterone by blocking renin; washout prevents hyperkalemia
Increases cAMP by inhibiting PDE3; washout prevents arrhythmia
e: Correct. Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, which degrades ANP, BNP and bradykinin; combining it with an ACE inhibitor greatly raises angioedema risk.
Wrong. The second drug is not an ACE inhibitor.
cl: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
combination tablet containing an angiotensin receptor blocker and a second drug
wait 36 hours after the last ACE inhibitor dose
Avoid overlap of ACE and neprilysin inhibition.
q.ch: Sacubitril blocks neprilysin → ↑ natriuretic peptides (vasodilation, natriuresis) and ↑ bradykinin → with an ACE inhibitor, bradykinin accumulates → angioedema → 36-hour washout.
q.tr: "Neprilysin Nibbles natriuretic peptides"; block it and they stay.
q.q2: The second drug increases which substances, and why is the washout needed?

q.s: A 64-year-old man with heart failure (ejection fraction 30%) is in sinus rhythm with a resting heart rate of 82/min despite the maximal tolerated dose of a β-blocker. A drug is added that lowers his heart rate without changing blood pressure or contractility. A month later he reports seeing brief flashes of bright light in dim settings.
o: L-type Ca2+ channels in the myocardium
The funny current (If) in the SA node
e: Correct. Ivabradine blocks HCN channels, slowing phase 4 depolarization in SA nodal cells; luminous phenomena (phosphenes) result from similar channels in the retina.
Wrong. He is already on a maximal β-blocker.
cl: Ivabradine only works in sinus rhythm.
lowers his heart rate without changing blood pressure or contractility
brief flashes of bright light in dim settings
q.ch: HFrEF + high resting rate despite β-blocker + pure rate slowing + phosphenes → ivabradine → blocks If (HCN) in the SA node.
q.tr: "IVabradine slows the If" — and makes you see stars.
q.q2: The added drug acts on which target?

q.s: A 63-year-old man with stable angina uses sublingual nitroglycerin. He takes a medication he did not mention for erectile dysfunction and, 4 hours later, uses nitroglycerin for chest pain. He becomes dizzy and his blood pressure falls to 70/40 mm Hg.
o: Both drugs block L-type Ca2+ channels
Both drugs increase cAMP in vascular smooth muscle
Nitrates raise cGMP via NO while the other drug blocks cGMP breakdown, causing excessive vasodilation
e: Correct. PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) potentiate nitrate-induced cGMP accumulation; the combination is contraindicated.
cl: a medication he did not mention for erectile dysfunction
blood pressure falls to 70/40 mm Hg
q.ch: Nitrate → NO → guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP; PDE5 inhibitor → ↓ cGMP breakdown → massive vasodilation → hypotension.
q.tr: "Nitrates + 'nafils' = never" (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil).
q.q2: Which mechanism explains the severe hypotension?

q.s: A 52-year-old man under spinal anesthesia becomes hypotensive (82/50 mm Hg) with a heart rate of 88/min. An intravenous drug is given. Within a minute, blood pressure rises to 128/80 mm Hg, and his heart rate falls to 58/min.
e: Wrong. Renal vasodilation; does not cause reflex bradycardia.
Wrong. A β-agonist that increases heart rate and can lower blood pressure.
Correct. A pure α1-agonist raises SVR and blood pressure; baroreceptors respond with a reflex fall in heart rate.
Wrong. Increases heart rate and contractility.
Wrong. Raises both blood pressure and heart rate.
cl: blood pressure rises to 128/80 mm Hg
Reflex bradycardia via the baroreceptor reflex.
q.ch: Pure α1-agonist → ↑ SVR → ↑ BP → baroreceptors fire more → ↑ vagal tone → reflex bradycardia.
q.tr: "Phenylephrine Pushes pressure up, Pulls rate down."
q.q2: Which drug was most likely given?

q.s: A 74-year-old man has exertional dyspnea. ECG shows a wide QRS complex (160 ms) with a broad, notched R wave in leads I and V6. On auscultation, the two components of S2 are heard more distinctly during expiration and merge into a single sound during inspiration.
o: Delayed closure of the aortic valve from left bundle branch block
Pulmonary hypertension with a loud P2
Delayed closure of the pulmonic valve from right bundle branch block
Early closure of the aortic valve from mitral regurgitation
Equal right and left atrial pressures from an atrial septal defect
e: Correct. Late LV activation delays A2 so that P2 comes first; inspiration delays P2 toward A2, narrowing the split (paradoxical splitting). Aortic stenosis can do the same.
Wrong. Causes a loud P2 but not paradoxical splitting.
Wrong. RBBB causes wide splitting that widens further with inspiration.
Wrong. Normally the split widens with inspiration.
cl: broad, notched R wave in leads I and V6
The split is widest in expiration: reversed from normal.
merge into a single sound during inspiration
Inspiratory delay of P2 closes the reversed gap.
q.ch: LBBB → delayed LV contraction → A2 after P2 → inspiration delays P2 toward A2 → split narrows on inspiration (paradoxical).
q.tr: "Paradoxical = Problems on the left (LBBB, aortic stenosis); Wide = Right bundle; Fixed = atrial hole."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains this pattern of S2 splitting?
